places.name: 姫路タンメン (Himeji Tanmen)
places.neighborhood: 駅前町 (Himeji Station north exit, 1-minute walk)

noodles.notes: Flat-cut thick noodles (平打ちの太麺) with real chew — chosen so the noodle can be found again under 360g of vegetables rather than lost in them. One local guide instead describes them as medium-thin and straight, so the gauge is not fully settled; the flat-thick reading is the better-attested one.

ramen.signature_bowl: Himeji Tanmen, ¥790. A clear chicken-and-pork chintan drawn slowly at low temperature and seasoned with salt, then 360 grams of vegetables — a full day's recommended intake — blasted in a wok over high heat and tipped in the moment they hit the soup, so the cabbage and bean sprouts arrive still squeaking. Over the top goes a heap of minced raw ginger. Miso tanmen (¥890), mapo tanmen (¥890), a meat-loaded niku tanmen (¥990) and a soupless abura soba (¥790) run alongside; you can ask for more vegetables, or for the vegetables without the noodles.
ramen.chashu: There is no sliced chashu — and that absence is the point. Tanmen's protein arrives cooked into the stir-fry rather than laid on top, so what you get is the pork that came out of the wok with the cabbage, wearing the same sear. The ¥990 niku tanmen doubles down on it; the standard bowl leaves the vegetables in charge.
notable_toppings: table ginger-shoyu (fresh grated and minced ginger, made daily)
house garlic steeped in soy and oil

gf.note: Wheat chukamen, and the wok seasoning and table ginger-shoyu are wheat soy sauce. No gluten-free option.

vegan.note: The broth is chicken and pork bone — true even of the noodle-free vegetable order.

ramen.pantheon: Tanmen is a Kantō invention — stir-fried vegetables over a salt soup — and by rights it has no business being a Himeji signature at all. What made it one is ginger. Himeji was once ginger-growing country, and this shop rebuilt the dish around that: minced raw ginger heaped on the bowl, a ginger-shoyu ground fresh every day at the table, garlic steeped in soy and oil beside it. Three separate ways to escalate the same heat. The soul underneath is a genuinely restrained one — chicken and pork bones held at low temperature so the fat never emulsifies, giving a translucent, low-lipid chintan that would be almost austere if you drank it alone. That austerity is deliberate: it is a soup built to disappear behind vegetables and let ginger do the talking. So the bowl reads light and eats huge, and the sharp, warming finish is unlike any tanmen in Tokyo. Since 2017 this shop has effectively made 姫路タンメン a gotōchi-men in its own right, and the second branch in Fukusaki says the city agreed.

places.name: 新生軒 (Shinseiken)
places.neighborhood: Minamimachi / right by Sanyo-Himeji Stn

noodles.notes: Thin straight noodles, boiled deliberately soft — no koshi, no firmness ladder, no request taken. Softness is the period-correct texture for a 1960 chuka soba and the shop has never revisited it.

ramen.signature_bowl: 中華そば, ¥650 — and there is essentially nothing else to decide. The soup arrives genuinely transparent, salt-seasoned rather than soy, so light on first sip that it seems to be hiding something, then filling in with a quiet savour that keeps you going back. Thin soft noodles, four toppings, no aroma oil, no ajitama, no options. The whole menu is five lines and has not changed since 1960: ramen, wonton, wonton-men, gyoza, rice. Regulars reach straight for the white pepper.
ramen.chashu: Plain braised pork chashu, cut thin and laid flat — lean, gently sweet, seasoned to sit inside a salt soup without staining it. It is the exact opposite of the modern thick aburi slab: chashu here is a component of a balanced bowl rather than the reason for it, which is precisely the 1960 reading of the ingredient.

gf.note: Wheat chukamen; wontons and gyoza add more wheat. No gluten-free option.

vegan.note: Animal-stock broth with pork chashu; no plant-based bowl.

ramen.pantheon: The sign outside says らーめん店の元祖 — the original ramen shop — and in Himeji that claim is close to fair: Shinseiken opened in 1960 and has held the same narrow slot in the Minamimachi arcade, steps from Sanyō-Himeji Station, ever since, seventeen counter seats under walls of vintage photographs of the street outside. The bowl is a fossil in the best sense, an unimproved specimen of pre-boom Japanese chūka soba, and its distinguishing choice is salt. A shio tare on a clear stock in 1960 was the ordinary provincial answer, before Tokyo shoyu and then tonkotsu colonised the national palate, and it produces something the modern ramen map has almost no room for: a soup you can see the bottom of, with no oil cap, no aroma oil, no depth-chasing at all — just a clean savoury line and thin noodles boiled soft enough to slip down. The shop has never published what goes in the pot, so the chicken reading is an informed one rather than a documented fact. What is documented is the restraint, and the fact that a bowl this quiet has held a corner of the arcade for sixty-five years while everything around it turned over.

places.name: 驛麺 らぁ～めん京 山陽姫路駅店 (Ekimen Ramen Kyo Sanyo-Himeji Station)
places.neighborhood: 山陽姫路駅構内 (Inside Sanyo-Himeji Station)

noodles.notes: 京都熟成細麺 — thin noodles given a long low-temperature ageing before service, the chain's central technical claim. Ageing relaxes and evens the dough so a thin noodle keeps its bite in a broth heavy enough to soften it fast.

ramen.signature_bowl: 京らぁ～めん, ¥670 — the chain's Gion paitan (祇園白湯), a chicken-and-pork-bone broth boiled cloudy and finished with soy. The consensus description is さっぱりしているのにコクがある: it goes down cleaner than its colour promises, then thickens in the aftertaste as you work down the bowl. One slice of chashu and half an ajitama on top, thin aged noodles underneath. The station branch trades hard on value — the old 55 set at ¥550 has been replaced since the October 2025 renovation by a ¥660 bowl-and-rice combo and an ¥880 bowl-and-side.
ramen.chashu: A single slice of braised pork chashu — a station-kiosk portion, not a statement. This is a bowl built for a commuter with fifteen minutes before the Sanyō train, and the protein is scaled accordingly; the half ajitama beside it does as much of the work.

gf.note: Wheat chukamen and a wheat soy-sauce tare. No gluten-free option.

vegan.note: Chicken-and-pork-bone paitan with pork chashu and egg.

ramen.pantheon: Kyoto is not one ramen style but three — the light chicken-pork shoyu of Shinpuku Saikan and Honke Daiichi Asahi, the se-abura shoyu of Masutani, and the gelatinous kotteri of Tenkaippin — and this chain descends from a fourth, more recent idea: Gion paitan, chicken and pork bones boiled to cloudiness and sold as a Kyoto product. Ramen Kyō runs it out of a Gion flagship across Hyōgo, Kyoto, Nara and Shiga, so what you get beside the ticket gates at Sanyō-Himeji is a Kyoto bowl imported wholesale, with nothing of Himeji in it. Judge it as what it is: the honest chain paitan, thinner and cleaner than a Hakata tonkotsu because the chicken keeps it from turning porky, carried on a thin aged noodle that is the chain's real craft claim. It is the most useful ramen in the city for the traveller with a train to catch — second floor, beside the barrier, open until 22:00 — and the least regionally interesting one. Renamed 驛麺 ("station noodles") when it reopened after renovation in October 2025, which is exactly the right name for it.

noodles.notes: Fine wavy noodles (縮れ麺) — the crimped cut that catches and holds a thin dashi-led soup, which is exactly why a broth this light can still taste of something on every mouthful.

ramen.signature_bowl: 中華そば, ¥580, unchanged in character since 1946. The broth is 和風だし before it is anything Chinese — kombu and iriko, the same kelp-and-dried-sardine axis a Japanese kitchen builds miso soup on — finished with soy into a clear, pale-brown bowl. It is emphatically あっさり: no fat cap, no bones dominating, a shallow-drinking soup that tastes of the Seto Inland Sea and then gets out of the way. Order it as the locals do, as part of a shumai lunch set (around ¥720) with the sesame dumplings for dessert.
ramen.chashu: Not documented. No published account describes the chashu here, which is itself telling — at 東来春 the meat that people write about is the shumai, and the ramen is the quiet half of the pairing.
notable_toppings: handmade potato-starch shumai (ordered alongside, eaten with Worcestershire sauce)

gf.note: Wheat chukamen and wheat soy-sauce tare; shumai wrappers and the sauce add more. No gluten-free option.

vegan.note: The broth is built on iriko (dried sardine) dashi.

ramen.pantheon: 東来春 is where Himeji ramen effectively starts — founded in 1946 in a bombed-out city, an udon-and-fried-rice shop that fed people out of scraps, and locally credited as the origin of the town's chūka soba. Its bowl is the clearest statement of the Himeji idiom there is: a Chinese restaurant that never really built a Chinese broth, reaching instead for kombu and iriko, the dashi any Japanese kitchen already had, and seasoning it with soy. What comes out is closer in soul to a Seto Inland Sea noodle soup than to anything from the mainland — thin, saline, faintly sweet with kelp, the small dried fish giving a grey-green savour that a bone broth cannot fake. The wavy noodle is the correct body for it, crimped so a soup with no fat to cling with still coats every strand. The shop's other legend runs on the same wartime logic: shumai bound with potato starch rather than padded with meat, chewy where a Yokohama shumai is soft, eaten dipped in Worcestershire sauce in the Himeji manner. Eighty years on, both are still on the counter beside the original cash register.

noodles.notes: 自家製麺 — house-milled and cut on site, and the wheat aroma is the first thing people mention. Flat-cut, medium-thin, and finished soft rather than firm: reviewers reach for sōmen as the comparison, a slippery delicate strand that suits a clear soup and would be wrong in a heavy one.

ramen.signature_bowl: 醤油らぁ麺 — jidori chicken drawn clear, seasoned with wooden-barrel-brewed soy sauce, and finished with fragrant chicken oil. It is the shoyu ramen played straight: no gimmick, no fish smash, just a bright golden bowl where you can taste the barrel in the tare and the bird in the soup, with the house noodles' wheat scent rising off the top. The chashu bowl (¥1,600) or wonton bowl (¥1,500) are the fully-dressed versions. Beside it sit a 煮干らぁ麺 built for a rice finish, a limited 昆布水つけ麺 that took a Kansai prize at the 2023 Ultimate Ramen competition, a tantanmen, and まぜそばジャンキー with slow-braised Yamagata pork on thick house noodles.
ramen.chashu: The obsession of the shop: several different chashu on one bowl, each a different cut and each cooked a different way — low-and-slow braised, grilled chicken chashu, rolled pork — so the plate reads as a small tasting of methods rather than two matching slices. The maze-soba runs a soft-set version cut into the sauce. Order the chashu bowl and this is what you are paying the extra ¥100 for.
notable_toppings: multiple chashu cuts and cooking methods
grated ginger, offered as a flavour change

gf.note: House-milled wheat noodles and a wheat soy-sauce tare — the two things this shop is proudest of. No gluten-free option.

vegan.note: Jidori chicken broth with niboshi and chicken oil; every bowl carries meat.

ramen.pantheon: This is the modern Japanese shoyu bowl — the らぁ麺 school that came out of Tokyo in the 2010s and spread nationwide, defined not by a region but by an attitude: name your chicken, name your soy sauce, mill your own noodles, and let a clear soup carry it. Hiramatsu-san came to it late, sixteen years a corporate manager and six months of persuading his family before he opened, and the resulting bowl has the precision of a career change staked on one idea. The soul is a clear jidori chicken chintan with niboshi laid underneath for a low bitter hum, and the identity comes from the tare — kioke-jikomi soy sauce, fermented in cedar barrels rather than steel, which brings a rounder, woodier soy note than industrial shoyu and is audible in the finish. Chicken oil floats on top for aroma. The body is the shop's own noodle, soft and flat and smelling of raw wheat, a deliberately gentle strand at a moment when most of the country is chasing firmness. It is the bowl in Himeji that a ramen traveller from Tokyo would recognise as speaking their language — and, in a city whose native idiom is dashi-light chūka soba, an outsider's ramen done extremely well.

noodles.notes: 斎麺 — an original low-carbohydrate noodle (about 40% less sugar than a standard noodle) with vegetable matter kneaded into the dough, offered in three versions: ginger, ashitaba, and chlorella, the last two coming out green. The base flour is not published and carries no gluten-free claim; reduced-carb noodles are conventionally built by raising the protein/gluten fraction, so treat these as wheat.

ramen.signature_bowl: 生姜味噌斎ラーメン — a ginger-miso bowl, thick and concentrated, that arrives with a heat that works from the inside out rather than from chilli on the surface. You pick your noodle first (ginger, ashitaba or chlorella) and then your treatment: the hot ginger-miso soup, a warm oil-based abura soba, or 丹波菜齋, a chilled noodle salad dressed with taro, rice kōji and black vinegar. It comes as the 菜斎コース (¥1,850) with smoked salad and dessert; the Himeji-only ginger miso runs to ¥1,600 on its own.
ramen.chashu: None, and no substitute pretending to be one. There is no soy-meat slab here — the shop's trick is the mock egg, built from vegetable matter and set to read as a soft-boiled ajitama on top of the bowl. The protein role in this bowl is played by vegetables and by the noodle itself.

gf.note: The 斎麺 noodles carry no gluten-free claim and read as wheat; miso can carry barley. Only the packaged Ibuki sweets are confirmed allergen-free.

vegan.note: Fully plant-based — no animal fat, no katsuo or niboshi dashi, no egg or dairy anywhere on the menu.

ramen.pantheon: Not a ramen shop in the lineage sense, and it should be read as what it is: a vegan kitchen north of Himeji Castle, run by an owner who trained his eye on Kusumoto Katsuzō's Saidō in Jiyūgaoka, that happens to make its lunch centrepiece a bowl of noodles. Strip the animal out of ramen and the whole modular machine has to be rebuilt — no bones for body, no fish for the umami undertow, no chiyu or lard for aroma — and the answer here is to move the flavour into the noodle itself, kneading ginger, ashitaba or chlorella into the dough so the body of the bowl carries character the broth cannot. The soul is then ginger and miso: a thick fermented-bean soup pushed hard with ginger heat, which lands it, quite by accident, in the same conversation as 姫路タンメン across town — two Himeji bowls, both leaning on the ginger this region once grew, arriving from opposite directions. Expect the concentration and warmth of a good miso ramen and none of its fat; expect vegetables from Tamba, a mock egg that looks the part, and a bowl that is honest about being health cooking first and ramen second.
